frase_gancho.texto: A stone jaguar with an offering bowl on its back.

puente_narrativo.texto: We continue with another object linked to offerings, this time in the shape of an animal: a jaguar carrying a ritual vessel on its back.

guion_corto.texto: At the bottom of the bowl that this jaguar carries on its back, two gods pierce their ears to offer their own blood. They are Tezcatlipoca and Huitzilopochtli. The jaguar itself is a cuauhxicalli, a vessel for placing hearts and blood, a Mexica work from the Late Postclassic. It is crouched, with its ears pricked up, its jaws open and its claws extended, as if ready to pounce. The wall of the bowl is carved with eagle feathers and beads that represent water. The Mexica linked the jaguar with the night, the underworld and the earth. It is thought to have been paired with another cuauhxicalli in the shape of an eagle, the animal of the day and the sky. It was discovered in December 1901, beneath the house of the Marquis of Apartado, in the Historic Center.

guion_largo.texto:
The Ocelotl Cuauhxicalli is a stone jaguar with a vessel hollowed out of its back. It is a Mexica work from the Late Postclassic. It retains traces of red, ochre and black pigments, and with those colors the feline must have looked very different from how you see it today.

The animal is crouched, ready to pounce. Its ears are pricked up, its jaws are open and its claws are extended. The Mexica linked the jaguar with the night, the underworld and the earth. It is associated with Tepeyóllotl, Heart of the Mountain, a form of the god Tezcatlipoca.

The word cuauhxicalli names a vessel where hearts and blood were placed. Here it is the circular bowl on the back. Its inner wall is carved with bands of eagle feathers and with greenstone beads, which represent precious water. At the bottom appear the gods Tezcatlipoca and Huitzilopochtli. They pierce their ears to offer their own blood. For the Mexica, blood was the food of the gods, and offering it helped keep the world in motion.

This jaguar is thought to have been paired with another cuauhxicalli, this time in the shape of an eagle, found a short distance away. The eagle was the animal of the sky and the day, and the jaguar that of the night and the earth. Together they expressed the balance of the cosmos.

It was discovered in December 1901, beneath the house of the Marquis of Apartado. It stood on the streets of Argentina and Donceles, in the Historic Center of Mexico City.

texto: Look for the circular bowl hollowed out of the jaguar’s back.
Notice the pricked-up ears, the open jaws and the extended claws.
Inside the bowl, find the bands of feathers and the beads that represent water.

texto.Material: Basalt with red, ochre and black pigments
texto.Origin: Historic Center, Mexico City (Marquis of Apartado house)
texto.Dimensions: 94 cm high x 120 cm wide x 225 cm long

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Ocelotl Cuauhxicalli was a decorative sculpture for a ruler’s palace.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a cuauhxicalli, a ritual vessel where hearts and blood were placed. Its bowl, with feathers and beads representing water, shows this.
